operator_plays.name: Wholesale ISO Schedule A Interchange-Plus vs. Compliant Dual-Pricing & ATM Residual Spread
operator_plays.mechanism: Negotiate sponsor-approved ISO Schedule A buy-rates with low markup over interchange and network assessments, then earn disclosed processing residual spreads through compliant dual-pricing or cash-discount POS deployments and exclusive venue ATMs. Pursue recurring basis-point and surcharge income for the contractual residual term; no lifetime payout or universal debit surcharge permission is assumed.
inputs: Executed sponsor-bank or processor ISO agreement and Schedule A defining buy-rates, residual ownership, reserves and termination rights
Merchant-approved POS configuration with legally reviewed cash and card pricing, signage, receipts and debit treatment
Exclusive venue ATM agreements with compliant fee disclosures, approved cash sourcing and remote operational telemetry
workflow: 1. Negotiate and document processing buy-rates, residual calculations, sponsor approval and enforceable payout and portfolio rights.
2. Underwrite merchants and configure genuine dual pricing or cash discounts under current network, debit and local-law requirements.
3. Deploy approved POS terminals and venue ATMs with clear customer disclosures, PCI controls and reconciled settlement and cash processes.
4. Audit monthly residuals and ATM surcharges against transaction reports, track attrition and correct pricing or disclosure exceptions promptly.
metrics: Net retained processing basis points after Schedule A costs, assessments and adjustments
Monthly net ATM surcharge contribution after venue splits, cash servicing and network costs
Merchant retention rate and residual statement reconciliation variance

platform_risks.failure_mode: Pricing misconfiguration or noncompliant disclosures trigger sponsor or card-network enforcement
platform_risks.trigger: Prohibited debit surcharge, misleading cash-discount presentation or unapproved merchant processing activity
platform_risks.impact: Refund obligations, fines, residual withholding and merchant or ISO termination
platform_risks.detection_metric: Pricing audit exceptions, customer fee complaints and sponsor compliance notices
platform_risks.fallback: Disable the disputed pricing configuration, restore approved transparent pricing and remediate with the sponsor before resuming the program

chapters.question_prompt: Who are the players in a card transaction, how does a payment actually move, and how has the Durbin Amendment changed debit interchange?
chapters.title: How Card Processing Works: Players, Payment Flow, and Debit Regulation
chapters.subtitle: Banks, ISOs, ISVs, and agents; authorization and settlement flow; ISO 20022 straight-through processing; merchant account statuses; day-to-day merchant support; and the Durbin Amendment's debit interchange cap, repeal campaigns, and rule changes
chapters.executive_summary: Merchant-services operators describe card acceptance as a fee-splitting machine: issuing banks collect interchange, Visa and Mastercard charge dues and assessments, processors and sponsoring banks move and settle funds, and ISOs hand agents the terminals, onboarding, and support so the agent only has to sell. Mario of Residual Builders runs the math: a $20,000-per-month cafe at 2.80% throws off $560 in fees, $280 goes to card costs, and an 80/20 split pays the agent $224 every month. Interchange-plus is the transparent default, while cash discounting and dual pricing reshaped the pitch after roughly 2016. On debit regulation, the Durbin cap of 21 cents plus 0.05% for banks over $10 billion split the room: James Shepherd and Transaction Expert say processors pocketed the windfall and small-ticket merchants got squeezed, while Cornerstone Advisors flags a further cut toward 14.4 cents.

key_metrics.label: Agent Residual on a $20,000-per-Month Merchant
key_metrics.value: $224 per month ($2,688 per year, $26,880 over 10 years)
key_metrics.context: Mario's cafe example: $560 in fees at 2.80%, $280 to card brands at 1.40%, $280 gross profit split 80/20 between agent and ISO or processor partner.

key_metrics.label: Durbin Regulated Debit Interchange Cap
key_metrics.value: 0.05% of the transaction plus 21 cents plus 1 cent for fraud protection
key_metrics.context: Cap applies to issuing banks with $10 billion or more in assets; smaller banks were not subject to it.

key_metrics.label: Proposed Fed Cut to the Debit Cap
key_metrics.metric: Proposed Fed Cut to the Debit Cap
key_metrics.value: 21 cents down to 14.4 cents, a 31% revenue hit
key_metrics.context: Kevin Von Holten says banks already over $10 billion lose 31%, while banks about to cross face a 60% to 70% impact.

key_metrics.label: Card-Present vs Card-Not-Present Rate Bands
key_metrics.value: About 1.25% to 2% card-present; about 2% to 3.5% card-not-present
key_metrics.context: Bryan Manning's general benchmarks; keyed, virtual-terminal, and online-form transactions price higher because of bank risk.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus — Who Touches the Swipe and Who Gets Paid
paragraphs: Joe Wagner breaks the card stack into fixed positions like a football roster. Issuing banks such as Chase or Wells Fargo put the card in the customer's hand, check available funds on every swipe, and collect interchange as their cut for fronting the money; acquiring banks sit at the finish line and deposit funds into the merchant's account minus fees. Visa, Mastercard, Discover, and American Express do not issue cards or hold money, they run the network and charge dues and assessments [N58l9UMrKHY @ 00:01:28]. Mario at Residual Builders draws the same map with more layers: processors like Fiserv, Elavon, and Global Payments move the data and settle, and behind every processor sits a sponsoring bank that is a member of the card networks, approves merchants, and supplies regulatory oversight [r78HBt5LE9U @ 00:05:14]. The flow Mario lays out runs in five beats: customer pays, request hits the processor, the networks query the issuer, the issuer approves or declines, and approved funds settle into the merchant account while fees peel off for every party [r78HBt5LE9U @ 00:06:28]. KULTURRA adds the gateway hop that routes card details to the right network before the processor talks to the customer's bank [QS1RtajZ0Yc @ 00:00:43].

Every practitioner who sells for a living agrees the agent should not become the bank. Joe Wagner says ISOs manage merchant accounts and build tailored solutions without processing payments themselves, and unless you want to be responsible for moving money around and following strict regulations, selling through an ISO is how to be successful [6dCPtuCCcvw @ 00:00:45]. In the roles breakdown, Wagner lists exactly what the ISO hands an agent: the terminals, the software, the customer service, the onboarding, and in many shops its own tech support and pricing models, which is why anyone selling merchant services is most likely working with or inside an ISO [N58l9UMrKHY @ 00:01:47]. Mario explains why so many agents choose an ISO over signing directly with a processor: the ISO is far more likely to do hand-holding, training, and support, which frees the agent to focus on marketing as the front-line sales force of the ecosystem [r78HBt5LE9U @ 00:03:23]. Mario also argues the ground is shifting under the generalist. Software companies, in Mario's words, are basically payment companies in disguise, and when processing is bundled with vertical software and modern hardware, payments become the organic, natural upsell instead of the whole pitch [lubvPaxm55o @ 00:13:30].

On debit regulation, the speakers line up on the baseline numbers even when they fight over the politics. All Things Money says the Durbin Amendment, passed in 2010 inside Dodd-Frank, capped debit interchange at 0.05% of the transaction plus 21 cents and an extra penny for fraud protection, applied only to banks with $10 billion or more in assets, and required issuing banks to use at least two unaffiliated networks so merchants can choose the most cost-effective path [F87ku5Df-mA @ 00:01:01]. CenturyPayments puts the before-and-after in plain terms: banks were charging retailers an average of 44 cents per debit transaction, collecting nearly $16 billion a year, and the cap that hit in October 2011 cut that to 21 cents [Jn1CXq7YPYs @ 00:00:50]. Kevin Von Holten at Cornerstone Advisors confirms the cliff from the issuer side, saying a bank crossing $10 billion watches blended debit interchange drop from roughly 38 or 39 cents to 21 cents [FwB1KshUr5A @ 00:00:19]. James Shepherd, an agent of North American Bank Card, frames the same math from the processor's ledger: the bank used to bill the processor about 1% plus 15 to 20 cents on a check card, and Durbin forced that down to 0.05% plus 21 cents [_5A2a4Vu7A8 @ 00:06:21].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Mario's cafe math is the cleanest unit-economics walk-through any of these operators gives. A coffee shop owned by John runs $20,000 a month in card sales at an illustrative 2.80% blended rate, which produces $560 in monthly fees [lubvPaxm55o @ 00:03:06]. The card brands take the first bite; at an assumed 1.40% average card cost that is $280, leaving $280 in gross profit to be split between the agent and the ISO or processor partner. On an 80/20 split the agent keeps $224 a month, $2,688 a year, and $26,880 over ten years for as long as John stays open [lubvPaxm55o @ 00:04:25]. Stack it and 10 clients pay $2,240 a month, 50 pay $11,200, and 100 pay $22,400. Mario also warns that every card carries a different cost, which is exactly why the pricing model matters. On interchange-plus, the agent shows the merchant the real cost of each of the 50 different card types on the statement and adds a disclosed margin, with Mario's own example being 0.60% on top of cost [r78HBt5LE9U @ 00:08:32]. James Shepherd runs the same structure at a thinner 0.25% markup and sets new clients up on nothing else [_5A2a4Vu7A8 @ 00:09:27].

Bryan Manning of BancardSales sets the rate benchmarks by acceptance environment. Card-present deals, where the card is swiped, dipped, or tapped including Apple Pay and Google Pay, run about 1.25% to 2%, while card-not-present deals keyed into a virtual terminal or entered on an online order form run about 2% to 3.5% because of the added bank risk [nLfsn6tUZh4 @ 00:04:44]. Manning budgets countertop terminals such as the VeriFone VX520 or Ingenico ICT220 at roughly $150 to $400, and a Clover point-of-sale build at about $1,000 depending on units and features [nLfsn6tUZh4 @ 00:02:52]. Mario lays out the menu agents pitch against those costs: interchange-plus, the older tiered model that buckets swipes into qualified, mid-qualified, and non-qualified, cash discounting released around 2016, and dual pricing, which displays both the card and cash price and became hugely popular in restaurants and retail. Tiered was the historical standard until merchants and agents moved toward transparent cost-plus [r78HBt5LE9U @ 00:09:25]. Shepherd puts real numbers on the tiered and flat-rate trap for debit: merchants typically pay 1.5% to 2% plus an 18 to 30 cent transaction fee, sometimes 35 cents, so a $100 check-card sale costs roughly $2 to $3 [_5A2a4Vu7A8 @ 00:04:02].

The Durbin math is where agents find their sharpest pitch. Shepherd walks a $100 check-card sale: the bank used to charge the processor about $1 plus 15 to 20 cents, the cap cut that to 0.05% plus 21 cents, or 26 cents, yet nothing stopped a flat-rate processor from still billing 2%, pocketing an extra 74 cents per transaction [_5A2a4Vu7A8 @ 00:07:29]. Shepherd's verdict on flat-rate processors is blunt: do not trust them to hand back that windfall. Transaction Expert, quoting a 22-cent per-item fee plus 0.05% against an old 1% to 1.2%, splits merchants by ticket size: under about $10, coffee, pizza, and hot dog shops saw the fixed fee jump from 10 cents to 22 cents, roughly doubling debit cost, while tickets above about $30 got cheaper, with large-ticket merchants due 20% to 30% savings [cL-wn0WX_PA @ 00:02:53]. Walmart and Target pay interchange directly, but merchants under a million dollars a month in volume go through a processor that Durbin never forced to pass anything along [cL-wn0WX_PA @ 00:04:13]. On the issuer side, Kevin Von Holten reports the Fed moving the 21-cent figure toward 14.4 cents, a 31% hit for banks already over $10 billion and 60% to 70% for banks about to cross [FwB1KshUr5A @ 00:01:15].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split on the debit side is over who actually pocketed the Durbin money. CenturyPaymentsInc frames it as a clean merchant win: banks were charging retailers an average of 44 cents per debit transaction, the cap dropped that to 21 cents in October 2011, and the merchant walks away with lower bank charges and room to cut prices [Jn1CXq7YPYs @ 00:01:11]. All Things Money flips that verdict, citing George Mason University research showing small businesses saw no reduction in interchange fees and consumers saw minimal savings, while large retailers negotiated lower merchant service charges and kept the spread [F87ku5Df-mA @ 00:02:45]. The Electronic Payments Coalition goes further, claiming more than three-fourths of merchants never changed prices after implementation and 22 percent actually raised them, a six to eight billion dollar yearly 'merchant markup' [MXBPDGL9Iss @ 00:01:02]. Transaction Expert splits the difference with a ticket-size rule: if the average ticket runs about $30 or more, the check card got cheaper, and a large-ticket shop should have seen costs fall by 20 to 30 percent, while below that line the fixed per-item fee did the damage [cL-wn0WX_PA @ 00:03:09]. The operator takeaway is that the same law reads as a windfall or a tax depending on ticket size and on who sits between the merchant and the issuing bank.

On pricing, the playbooks diverge sharply. James Shepherd of Multi-Merchant Processing runs a hard line: only interchange plus for every new client, passing through whatever the bank charges plus 0.25 percent, so when Durbin cut the issuer cost those merchants automatically captured 100 percent of the drop [_5A2a4Vu7A8 @ 00:09:27]. Mario at Residual Builders also ran interchange plus for many years, but pitched a fatter 0.60 percent margin on top of the card cost and sold it as the most transparent model on the statement, because the merchant sees each card type, its cost, and the agent margin [r78HBt5LE9U @ 00:08:48]. Joe Wagner pushes a different angle, telling agents their responsibility is to educate merchants on dual pricing or cash discounting while making sure they carry the best technology [6dCPtuCCcvw @ 00:00:45]. Mario then undercuts the cash discount pitch itself: after roughly ten years in market, most owners either already pass fees to customers or know the program and refuse it, so the novelty is gone and the industry is leaving what Mario calls phase three [lubvPaxm55o @ 00:12:21]. The practical fork is clear: interchange plus wins the transparency and Durbin pass-through argument, fee-passing programs win the total-savings argument, and the newest operators treat both as table stakes rather than the hook.

The second fork is structural: where an agent plugs in and how wide they sell. Joe Wagner is blunt that unless you want to move the money and carry strict regulations yourself, selling through an ISO is how you succeed, and they tell reps not to overcomplicate the role [6dCPtuCCcvw @ 00:01:01]. Residual Builders agrees on the ISO path for most newcomers, noting that an ISO is far more likely to provide hand-holding, training, and support than a direct payment processor would, which is why many agents choose to work under one [r78HBt5LE9U @ 00:03:23]. Where Mario parts ways with the keep-it-simple camp is positioning: the days of the generalist, and of selling savings and support, are counted, and phase four belongs to vertical software where payment processing becomes the organic natural upsell [lubvPaxm55o @ 00:14:04]. Joe Wagner's own roles breakdown lands closer to Mario than the simplicity pitch suggests, calling ISVs that build booking apps and restaurant point of sale systems with integrated payments an increasingly powerful distribution partner for agents [N58l9UMrKHY @ 00:02:44]. The real split is not whether ISOs matter but whether a bare rate pitch still opens doors, or whether software now has to carry the conversation.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The sharpest trap on the merchant side is the small-ticket squeeze. Transaction Expert says coffee shops, pizza shops, and hot dog stands with tickets under $10 'really got screwed,' because the fixed per-item fee on a check card jumped from 10 cents to 22 cents, roughly doubling the cost of every small debit swipe [cL-wn0WX_PA @ 00:02:53]. The Electronic Payments Coalition makes the same point from the opposite camp: the corner shop now pays the same capped amount on a $5 sandwich that Walmart pays on a $1,000 TV [MXBPDGL9Iss @ 00:00:47]. The second trap is the processor windfall. James Shepherd walks a $100 check card sale through it: the bank's charge to the processor fell from about one dollar to 26 cents, but a merchant on tiered or flat rate still pays the contracted two percent, so the processor pockets an extra 74 cents and carries no legal duty to pass it down [_5A2a4Vu7A8 @ 00:07:29]. BestCardProcessing reports the same pattern after implementation, with small and mid-sized merchants who are not enrolled in a specific pinpoint rate program simply not receiving the intended savings, and some processing companies unable to even offer that program [UMy8ceQ1bm4 @ 00:12:16].

On the issuer side, the failure mode is the $10 billion cliff. Cornerstone Advisors puts the drop for a bank crossing the line at a blended 38 to 39 cents down to 21 cents, and says the Fed's move to 14.4 cents means a 31 percent hit for banks already over, but a 60 to 70 percent impact for anyone approaching the threshold [FwB1KshUr5A @ 00:01:15]. They sized it for a $9.9 billion client holding 269,000 debit cards: to cross $10 billion and keep revenue flat it would need 498,000 more active cards, 188 percent growth, which they call impossible, forcing 30 different mitigation strategies while clients scramble to stay under the mark [FwB1KshUr5A @ 00:02:46]. CenturyPaymentsInc warned at launch that with such a loss in revenue, banks would most likely look for ways to make up that money somewhere else [Jn1CXq7YPYs @ 00:01:27]. The Electronic Payments Coalition says that is exactly what happened, with community banks, credit unions, and consumers carrying the burden through eliminated debit card rewards and free checking accounts [MXBPDGL9Iss @ 00:01:37]. For anyone whose economics ride on debit volume, the lesson is that capped issuer revenue flows downhill into fees and cuts elsewhere in the chain.

The back-office traps are less dramatic but cost real money. NMI warns that a past-due merchant left unresolved goes delinquent and gets locked out of their account, and if six months pass without collecting gateway fees, the balance is debited from the reseller's own affiliate account [WxBDVPgeUYI @ 00:01:43]. Bryan Manning of BancardSales flags setup errors: the wrong SIC or MCC code, or a miscategorized processing method, can leave a merchant paying higher rates than they otherwise qualify for, on top of the reality that a merchant account is effectively a short-term loan paid out before the cardholder settles their bill [nLfsn6tUZh4 @ 00:06:37]. ECS Payments says the most common support call is a variance between the merchant's settlement report and the processor's, usually an unnoticed refund, while charges from software like QuickBooks show up four to five times a week as phantom debits [NXWIjxZTNpI @ 00:07:26]. And for anyone eyeing the ATM side of this volume, Mario at Residual Builders calls ATM placement close to merchant services but heavy, expensive to buy, constantly needing cash loaded, often demanding a location profit share, with some locations that simply perform badly [lubvPaxm55o @ 00:08:22].

callout.title: Four Checks Before You Promise a Merchant Debit Savings
callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss, lockout, or overcharge a practitioner saw firsthand. Clear all four before quoting savings or boarding the account.
items: Confirm the merchant is on interchange plus, because a processor holding a flat-rate contract is not going to hand over the Durbin windfall on its own [durbinamendment — _5A2a4Vu7A8 @ 00:10:36].
Pull the average ticket first: under $10 the 22-cent per-item fee raises costs, while around $30 and above the cap actually saves money [Transaction Expert — cL-wn0WX_PA @ 00:02:41].
Resolve any past-due gateway account immediately so it never goes delinquent and the balance is never debited from your affiliate account [NMI — WxBDVPgeUYI @ 00:05:02].
Verify the SIC or MCC code and card-present versus card-not-present setup, since miscoding means paying higher rates than the merchant qualifies for [BancardSales — nLfsn6tUZh4 @ 00:06:37].

chapters.pull_quote: "It capped the amount of money that the bank can charge the processor, but it missed something very, very important: it did not tell the processor what they could charge to you, the business owner." — durbinamendment (_5A2a4Vu7A8 @ 00:07:09)
action_checklist: Pull every merchant statement and run a cost analysis on any account that has not had one in the last twelve months, since the processor may have kept the reduced debit cost as profit [Transaction Expert — cL-wn0WX_PA @ 00:04:53].
Board new merchants on interchange plus with a fixed markup such as plus 0.25 percent, so any drop in bank charges passes through automatically [durbinamendment — _5A2a4Vu7A8 @ 00:09:46].

Model each deal before signing: $20,000 monthly volume at 2.80 percent is $560, minus $280 card cost leaves $280 gross, and an 80/20 split pays $224 per month [Residual Builders — lubvPaxm55o @ 00:04:25].
Code the SIC or MCC and the card-present or card-not-present environment correctly at setup so the merchant lands in the lowest rate category they qualify for [BancardSales — nLfsn6tUZh4 @ 00:06:37].
Watch the gateway list accounts page for pending, past due, and delinquent tags and clear failed fee charges before six months of non-collection hits your own account [NMI — WxBDVPgeUYI @ 00:01:43].

Give merchants the list of debit descriptors and have their merchant ID ready on support calls so reconciliation and bank-statement questions get resolved fast [ECS Payments — NXWIjxZTNpI @ 00:06:58].

chapters.question_prompt: How do interchange, tiered, flat-rate, interchange-plus, and subscription pricing compare, and how do you read a merchant statement to find the real cost?
chapters.title: Merchant Pricing Models and Statement Analysis
chapters.subtitle: Interchange basics; tiered vs. interchange-plus vs. flat-rate vs. subscription pricing; which structure pays the agent more; and reading tiered and cost-plus statements line by line to find hidden fees
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners across BancardSales, CCSalesPro, Merchant Maverick, Helcim and MerchantAccounts.ca agree that interchange is the fixed wholesale floor under every pricing model, identical across processors and non-negotiable, so the only lever is the processor markup and the card-acceptance habits that keep transactions in cheaper categories. The street mechanics are statement math: total interchange divided by volume should land near 1.7 percent, total fees minus interchange exposes markup, and tier statements are judged by card mix before rates, with 60 to 70 percent qualified expected for storefronts. Agents price from Schedule A costs, using per-item fees to survive small-ticket debit. The split comes on tiered pricing: Merchant Maverick and Joe Wagner call it a buried-markup red flag, while Bryan Manning and Paygent AI argue the right model is situational, with Manning naming the effective rate as the only undisputed yardstick.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner starts from the same floor: interchange. Bryan Manning of BancardSales frames it as the prime rate of payments, a published schedule of hundreds of categories that is the same for every processing company and acts as the base cost for credit and debit acceptance [AseZioaNb5s @ 00:01:14]. Ahmad at Merchant Maverick calls it the wholesale layer set by Visa and Mastercard, shared between the card associations and issuing banks like Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, and flatly states those fees cannot be negotiated [h72ua8pD9cU @ 00:04:38]. David at MerchantAccounts.ca makes the same point from the Canadian side: interchange is set at a country level, so switching processors never changes the underlying cost structure, and nearly all of it flows to the card issuing bank with a roughly 0.1 percent card brand fee layered on top [btemhvIers4 @ 00:00:47]. PaymentCloud closes the loop for the merchant across the desk: because issuing banks assign interchange, there is no way to lower it, but the discount rate the processor adds to each transaction is open for negotiation [xfBalp9Zzio @ 00:06:31]. The practical consensus is blunt. The only money in play is the markup, so every pitch, audit and repricing targets that layer and nothing beneath it.

The practitioners also agree on what pushes a transaction into a cheap or expensive category. Manning lists the business type and MCC code, face-to-face versus internet acceptance, average ticket, consumer versus business or corporate cards, interchange optimization technology and daily settlement, noting each card lands in one and only one category and that the brands publish changes twice a year, spring and fall [AseZioaNb5s @ 00:02:37]. Merchant Maverick puts a ratio on the card-type gap: credit interchange runs roughly six times higher than debit, rewards cards cost more, and interchange eats roughly 70 to 90 percent of total processing cost depending on the rate plan [dUz90pAXTm0 @ 00:02:30]. James Shepherd of CCSalesPro adds the industry layer most merchants miss, explaining that the same card spending 100 dollars costs a grocery store less than a retail store because grocers run on their own interchange table, while B2B cards and rewards cards cost more and debit usually costs significantly less except at tiny-ticket shops like coffee [bdumFSr4sA8 @ 00:04:25]. Manning turns that into merchant-side habits: run AVS, key the three-digit code and billing zip, settle daily, swipe or dip whenever the card is present, and void instead of refunding, all to qualify more transactions into the lower interchange category [AseZioaNb5s @ 00:04:57].

The third point of agreement is that the processor's underlying cost never moves with the pricing label on the account. Shepherd tells a newly independent agent that whether a 10,000 dollar pizza shop sits on interchange plus, tiered, flat rate, surcharging or cash discounting, the roughly 200 dollars of interchange plus dues, assessments and Schedule A per-item costs stays identical, so revenue depends entirely on how the deal is priced [fb0PHmE8aCc @ 00:01:07]. Shepherd reduces the choice to simplicity versus transparency: larger accounts want interchange plus not because it is cheaper but because the statement shows cost and markup line by line, while smaller merchants are drifting from tiered to a single flat rate because they do not want fifty lines on a statement [fb0PHmE8aCc @ 00:02:51]. David at MerchantAccounts.ca lands in the same place, saying flat pricing can suit a small merchant who mostly wants easy reconciliation, but every large merchant on the planet belongs on interchange plus [btemhvIers4 @ 00:04:58]. Manning's tiebreaker is the effective rate: every model collapses into one end-of-month number, and that rate is the only undisputed figure for comparing any two providers [5jk-0XxkiR0 @ 00:11:32]. In practice, operators read every model through that single number before arguing about labels.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Statement work starts with identifying the pricing model in seconds, before touching a single rate. Shepherd's rule for tiered statements is to scan for qualified, mid-qualified and non-qualified, usually abbreviated as qual, m-qual and n-qual, and the presence of those words alone confirms tier pricing [RxgrRsVThx4 @ 00:00:00]. An interchange plus statement instead carries a huge interchange table of incomprehensible abbreviations, anywhere from ten to 200 lines, plus a total interchange figure; Shepherd treats a supposed cost-plus statement with no total interchange amount as suspicious on sight [2Sn4XMqpW4I @ 00:05:13]. The disguise to watch for is tiered pricing dressed up as an interchange table: the category names are real, but scanning down the rate column shows only three or four distinct rates repeating across many lines, which means bucketed rates are being displayed like pass-through [XEaaN73nJ6Q @ 00:06:39]. Subscription pricing announces itself as one large monthly subscription or monthly fee around 40 or 50 dollars, with everything else presented as Visa and Mastercard cost, though Shepherd warns that small network-access fees often carry hidden markup on top of the subscription, and that processors mostly offer it to small merchants who would pay only about 30 dollars of markup on tiered pricing, overpaying roughly 20 dollars a month [aZv0u_x9ipQ @ 00:00:42].

Once the model is known, the arithmetic is simple enough to run at a counter. Shepherd divides total interchange by total volume and expects roughly 1.7 percent, with 1.6 to 1.8 percent normal, small-ticket debit-heavy shops near 2.5 to 2.7 percent, large-ticket rewards and B2B merchants around 2.2 to 2.8 percent, and debit-heavy auto repair as low as 1 percent [2Sn4XMqpW4I @ 00:03:03]. Total fees minus total interchange is the markup; divide that by volume and benchmark it against size: 1 to 1.5 percent is unremarkable under 10,000 dollars a month, anything over about 0.7 percent at 20,000 to 40,000 is uncompetitive, and above 60,000 even 0.3 percent probably has a better offer waiting [2Sn4XMqpW4I @ 00:06:22]. David shows the per-card math in Canada: a basic Visa at 1.4 percent interchange plus a 0.1 percent card brand fee is a 1.5 percent cost, so interchange plus 0.5 percent bills the merchant 2 percent on that card [btemhvIers4 @ 00:02:07]. The markup ladder then steps down with size, with David quoting around 0.25 over interchange at a million dollars a month for low-risk product and about 0.15 at ten million [btemhvIers4 @ 00:03:42].

On tiered statements, Shepherd's first move is card mix, not rates: a storefront retailer, restaurant or auto shop should show 60 to 70 percent qualified with the rest split roughly evenly between mid and non-qualified, and anything lower usually means savings are sitting on the table [RxgrRsVThx4 @ 00:02:54]. The quickest rate win is converting a blended qualified rate into four-tier pricing with a separate, cheaper debit and check card qualified rate. On the agent side, the CCSalesPro coach dissects a live deal priced at 1.45, 2.29 and 3.5 percent plus 10 and 15 cent item fees: with regulated debit costing about 22 cents and five basis points, that 25 cents covers the per-item cost and the qualified basis points on debit are almost all profit [fb0PHmE8aCc @ 00:06:41]. For a 240 dollar average ticket, the play is interchange plus 40 basis points and 10 cents for a large account, or for one doing 20,000 dollars a month or less, a simplified flat 2.15 percent and 25 cents, keeping a high per-item fee because nothing else is passed through [fb0PHmE8aCc @ 00:08:16]. The coach's final call was to simply match the existing tiered pricing, because the mid and non-qualified bumps protect margin if next month brings rewards and corporate cards instead of debit [fb0PHmE8aCc @ 00:10:06].

callout.title: Street-Level Pricing Edges From the Field
callout.body: These are the moves practitioners use to protect margin on their own book and to find switch targets fast on someone else's statement.
items: Never price an average ticket under about 15 dollars on flat or tiered without a per-item fee; agents who sold a coffee shop at 3.5 percent flat owed the processor money on the first residual [CCSalesPro — fb0PHmE8aCc @ 00:05:24]

A merchant still on tiered pricing likely has not had fees reviewed in years and is almost always overpaying, which makes the account a prime switch target [Joe Wagner | Merchant Services & Passive Income — XXH81AbZQcg @ 00:01:11]

Before switching processors, ask the current one to move the account onto interchange plus, since the same processor may offer all three models and cut fees without a switch [Paygent AI — xTWy5shtdSk @ 00:09:53]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Tiered pricing is the sharpest split on the street. Ahmad at Merchant Maverick calls it the least transparent model and the worst one a merchant can sit on. He tells owners to ask their processor whether they are on it and to get off it immediately [h72ua8pD9cU @ 00:16:08]. Joe Wagner goes further for agents prospecting accounts. To him tiered is old school and intentionally vague, and a merchant still on it is a great sign, because they likely have not had their fees reviewed in years and are almost always overpaying [XXH81AbZQcg @ 00:01:11]. Bryan Manning at BancardSales pushes back hard. He rejects the claim that tier-based and flat rate programs are dishonest. He points out that Stripe and Square both boldly claim transparent pricing on their own pricing pages while running tier-based models, and concludes that true and transparent is just a subjective term people use for whatever model they prefer [5jk-0XxkiR0 @ 00:10:17]. CCSalesPro sits in between. When the host started fifteen years ago everybody was on tiered. It faded, then came back in a resurgence. Today the most common version is two-tier pricing, card present versus card not present, the structure PayPal, Square and Stripe run [XEaaN73nJ6Q @ 00:04:26].

Interchange plus gets the loudest endorsements, but even its champions make exceptions. David at MerchantAccounts.ca calls it the best model in the industry with literally no downside. He would quote a low-risk merchant doing a million dollars a month at 0.25 over interchange and a ten-million-dollar account at 0.15. He still concedes it is not always best for small merchants who just want something easy to reconcile, and flat pricing may suit them better [btemhvIers4 @ 00:04:58]. Helcim pitches scale: at 100K in monthly sales, an interchange plus merchant could see an effective rate under 1.5%, compared with the 2.5% or 2.9% Square or Stripe keep charging as volume grows [cZ2DaswdAqo @ 00:08:22]. Crystal Little at Paygent AI flips the flat-rate argument. She says card-not-present e-commerce shops benefit most from flat rate because their underlying interchange is already the highest. She even recommends splitting volume across two processors: interchange plus for in-person payments and a flat rate processor online [xTWy5shtdSk @ 00:12:34]. Subscription pricing draws the widest split. CCSalesPro flags that processors mostly hand it to small merchants who would pay only thirty dollars of markup on tier pricing instead of a fifty-dollar subscription, and that extra network-access fees get marked up on top [aZv0u_x9ipQ @ 00:01:19].

On the agent side, CCSalesPro's coaching call reframes the whole debate around the agent's own books. Schedule A costs (interchange, card brand dues and assessments, per-item costs and BIN sponsorship) are identical whether you sell interchange plus, tiered, flat rate, surcharging or cash discounting. That leaves revenue as the only question, and revenue depends entirely on the level you price at. Interchange plus 90 basis points and 25 cents earns a lot, while interchange plus five basis points and three cents earns almost nothing [fb0PHmE8aCc @ 00:01:57]. For a debit-heavy merchant with a 240-dollar average ticket, the coach lays out two plays. Go in with interchange plus 40 basis points and 10 cents if the account is big. Simplify to a flat 2.15% and 25 cents across the board if they run 20,000 a month or less [fb0PHmE8aCc @ 00:08:29]. Contract terms split practitioners too. David at MerchantAccounts.ca wants young merchants on month-to-month interchange plus, but tells larger established merchants to trade a longer contract term for a lower interchange markup [btemhvIers4 @ 00:05:27]. Ahmad at Merchant Maverick, by contrast, ranks the early termination fee among the worst junk fees. It runs from a hundred dollars to thousands, and he says good processors do not charge one [h72ua8pD9cU @ 00:11:00].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive agent mistake is pricing a small-ticket account on percentage alone. CCSalesPro tells of agents who sold a coffee shop a flat 3.5% across the board, opened their first residual statement, and found they had lost money and owed it back to the processor [fb0PHmE8aCc @ 00:04:39]. The math is brutal. Regulated debit under the Durbin amendment carries 22 cents, card brand fees add a couple of cents, and a five-cent transaction fee rides on top. That puts roughly 33 cents of fixed cost on a customer spending two dollars, about 15% of the ticket against a 3.5% charge [fb0PHmE8aCc @ 00:05:08]. The coach's rule is that once the average ticket drops below 15 bucks, flat or tier pricing needs real per-item fees built in, or it will eat your lunch in a hurry. The second trap is trusting a single month. A debit-heavy account showing a 1.99 effective rate looks safe to flat-price near two percent and 25 cents. But if that month was a fluke and the merchant starts running rewards and corporate cards at two and a half to three percent, the margin shrinks very quickly. The safer play is matching the existing tier sheet so the mid-qualified and non-qualified buckets protect the margin [fb0PHmE8aCc @ 00:09:50].

On the statement, the biggest error James Shepherd at CCSalesPro sees on tier pricing is reading the rates instead of the card mix. No industry rule says which transactions go into which bucket. Some processors post a really good qualified rate, put very few transactions there, and push most of the volume into non-qualified, the highest rate [RxgrRsVThx4 @ 00:02:40]. His benchmark is that a retailer, restaurant or auto repair shop should show 60% to 70% qualified, with the rest split fairly evenly between mid-qualified and non-qualified. A pizza shop's phone orders belong in mid-qualified, but anything far outside that pattern points to savings [RxgrRsVThx4 @ 00:02:54]. Interchange plus has its own trap. If the statement never shows a total interchange amount, Shepherd calls it suspicious. If total interchange divided by total volume sits far from the roughly 1.7% national average, it may be what he calls interchange plus plus: marked-up interchange with hidden costs buried in the table [2Sn4XMqpW4I @ 00:04:13]. The markup check is total fees minus total interchange, divided by volume. At 20,000 to 40,000 a month, a markup above about 0.7% is most likely not competitive. Even 0.3% at 60,000 and up can probably be beaten [2Sn4XMqpW4I @ 00:06:40].

Merchant-side traps cluster in the flat-fee lines. Ahmad at Merchant Maverick calls a terminal lease an absolutely horrible deal that ends up costing thousands of dollars for a 200 to 300 dollar piece of equipment. His rule is simple: don't ever get a terminal lease [h72ua8pD9cU @ 00:09:20]. PaymentCloud warns that many processors implement annual rate increases, usually announced by a notice on the statement two to three months before they hit. It tells merchants to watch leasing and equipment fees, compliance and regulatory fees, PCI fees and monthly access fees to make sure they do not creep up [xfBalp9Zzio @ 00:04:53]. The same team calls chargebacks financial gremlins that nibble away at profits and can ultimately get the merchant account terminated. High-risk accounts can also have a percentage of sales held in a separate non-interest-bearing reserve account [xfBalp9Zzio @ 00:03:25]. Merchant Maverick's Maverick Minute adds a red flag for sales pitches: be careful if a merchant account rep offers a discount on the standard published interchange rates. The only way to eliminate or reduce interchange is to pass it on to customers, which Merchant Maverick calls a whole other can of worms [dUz90pAXTm0 @ 00:03:58].

callout.title: Pre-Quote Kill Checks
callout.body: Run these four checks on every statement before you put a number in front of a merchant. Each one comes from a practitioner who watched an account or a margin blow up.
items: Never quote flat or tier pricing on an average ticket under 15 dollars without per-item fees that cover the 22-cent regulated debit cost [CCSalesPro — fb0PHmE8aCc @ 00:05:24].
Check card mix before rates: a physical-location statement running well under 60% to 70% qualified means the buckets are stacked against the merchant [CCSalesPro — RxgrRsVThx4 @ 00:02:54].
Treat any interchange plus statement without a total interchange figure as suspicious, then subtract interchange from total fees to expose the real markup [CCSalesPro — 2Sn4XMqpW4I @ 00:05:13].
Walk away from any rep promising a discount on standard published interchange rates, since interchange only goes away by passing it to customers [Merchant Maverick — dUz90pAXTm0 @ 00:03:58].

chapters.pull_quote: "You got to make sure you have some per item fees in there because if you don't that can really eat your lunch in a hurry." - CCSalesPro (fb0PHmE8aCc @ 00:05:39).
action_checklist: Calculate the effective rate (total fees divided by total volume) on every statement and use it as the single number to compare any two providers [BancardSales — 5jk-0XxkiR0 @ 00:11:32].
Divide total interchange by total volume and compare it against the roughly 1.7% average to catch marked-up interchange [CCSalesPro — 2Sn4XMqpW4I @ 00:03:03].
Subtract total interchange from total fees, divide by volume, and test that markup against the volume benchmarks before quoting [CCSalesPro — 2Sn4XMqpW4I @ 00:06:22].
On tier statements, move the merchant from one blended qualified rate to split debit and credit qualified rates on 4-tier pricing [CCSalesPro — RxgrRsVThx4 @ 00:06:55].
Strike junk fees: a statement fee charged on top of the monthly fee, online reporting fees, debit network fees, and monthly minimums negotiated to zero [Merchant Maverick — h72ua8pD9cU @ 00:11:27].

Push card acceptance best practices that qualify transactions for lower interchange: AVS, CVV and zip entry, daily settlement, swiping or dipping, and voids instead of refunds [BancardSales — AseZioaNb5s @ 00:05:14].

chapters.question_prompt: How do you cut processing costs for B2B and debit-heavy merchants through Level 2/3 data, interchange optimization, and the post-Durbin debit rules?
chapters.title: Interchange Optimization: Level 2/3 Data, Visa CEDP, and Debit Rate Rulings
chapters.subtitle: Level 2 and Level 3 card data; interchange audits; PayTrace optimization and Visa CEDP since April 2026; auto-filled data risk; a $35,000/month case study; gateway feature settings; the truck stop ruling against the Fed's debit cap; and whether processors pass Durbin savings through
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree interchange, not processor markup, is the margin pool: Sean Jones puts it at 75 to 90 percent of card fees, and VeraSave's Jeremy Layton says interchange drives 80 to 90 percent of delivered savings. Only business, corporate, purchasing and government cards benefit, via a Level 3-capable gateway. The street mechanics are statement-driven: flag standard and EIRF downgrades, fix batch timing, and pass real line items. Quoted Visa spreads run 75 to 120 basis points, and Jones reports one client saving $35,000 per month. Visa CEDP changed the rules: Level 2 programs retired in April 2026, a 0.05 percent fee now applies to enhanced-data transactions, and unverified merchants get no Level 3 rate. Practitioners split on whether Level 3 can be automatic, and the 8th Circuit's October 2026 debit ruling has not yet moved the 21 cent cap.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus: Interchange Is the Real Margin Pool
paragraphs: Every practitioner on this beat starts from the same arithmetic: the processor markup is the small number, and interchange is the big one. Sean Jones of Revolution Payments puts interchange at 75 to 90 percent of total card fees and stresses that this money flows back to the issuing bank, not the processor, across more than 400 distinct rates that shift by card type, processing method, ticket size and industry [vVvGM8Rlor8 @ 00:00:15]. Jeremy Layton of VeraSave lands in the same range, saying 80-plus percent of a merchant's fees are interchange, which is exactly why his shop aims at interchange rather than processor margin [KlaksrooZhw @ 00:07:56]. Jones adds the uncomfortable reason most merchants never hear about Level 3: processors earn nothing from interchange, and plenty of reps lack the knowledge because no certification is required to enter the field [QBl05xxHst0 @ 00:01:27]. James Sheppard of CCSalesPro frames the operator payoff bluntly. Facing a merchant who wanted lower costs, the choice was either to cut residuals and lose margin by lowering the pricing, or to find a way to cut the interchange costs, which cost the ISO nothing [AKvayIEwefA @ 00:33:36]. The consensus play is to attack the interchange category each transaction lands in while leaving the markup intact, so the merchant saves real money and the residual survives the conversation.

The second point of agreement is who actually benefits. TouchSuite is explicit that only business, corporate, purchasing and government cards gain from enhanced data, and that consumer cards generally do not, so the opportunity has to be sized against business-card volume alone [60QTYm0QFZU @ 00:00:22]. Roger McNamara, appearing on CCSalesPro, sharpens the filter further: about 30 percent of B2B transactions still do not qualify, because cards carrying personal liability are excluded from the commercial programs [tG2nIK3Th4Q @ 00:10:18]. The baseline prerequisite is the right pipe. Jones warns that credit card terminals do not support Level 3 line-item detail, and that a merchant needs a Level 3-capable payment gateway, which a competent processor should be able to help select [QBl05xxHst0 @ 00:02:31]. The final shared rule is that data has to be real and verified, not merely present in the authorization. PayTrace states it flatly under Visa's Commercial Enhanced Data Program: if you are not verified, you do not get Level 3 regardless of what you are trying to send in [5z1bCzU6Luw @ 00:26:40]. That turns Level 3 eligibility into a status the merchant earns rather than a toggle the gateway flips. Across channels the model is identical: identify commercial volume, route it through a capable gateway, and feed it data that survives Visa's scrutiny.

On the debit side, the consensus is about pass-through, not optimization tricks. Merchant Doctor warns that some processors will not pass Durbin savings to merchants and tells owners to look for qualified, mid-qualified and non-qualified buckets on their statements, then demand true interchange-plus pricing [Hx-TboJVDyo @ 00:02:58]. Sloan Bush of Interchange Plus Solutions, speaking with Practical Ecommerce, makes the same case with numbers: e-commerce debit interchange sat at 1.6 percent plus 15 cents while merchants were paying roughly 2.25 percent plus 30 cents, and tiered processors pocketed the difference [LjfmC9EATic @ 00:06:24]. The legal ground is shifting but has not moved checkout yet. LawLens reports the 8th Circuit ruled unanimously for the truck stop Corner Post on October 26, 2026, knocking down the Fed's debit-card fee cap [M4iOZn_3wng @ 00:01:30], yet stresses that no new fee was set, the Fed has roughly 45 days to seek rehearing, and until the mandate issues, the 21 cent cap stands [M4iOZn_3wng @ 00:04:36]. The operator takeaway shared by all three is the same: debit savings only reach a merchant whose pricing is true interchange-plus, because a tiered statement can absorb a rate cut before the merchant ever sees it. Whatever the courts eventually set, the statement structure decides who keeps the money.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The street workflow starts with the statement, not the pitch deck. TouchSuite's method is to find every line labeled business, corporate, purchasing or commercial, flag the standard and non-qualified lines, then compare a qualified line against a downgraded one to measure the rate gap [60QTYm0QFZU @ 00:00:40]. CCSalesPro's Payment Insights segment tells reps to hunt for standard or EIRF entries, with the standard downgrade rate sitting around 2.95 percent [mqEQN-xgAAk @ 00:03:33]. The same segment shows how cheap the fix can be: an auto shop doing over $100,000 a month had 80 percent of its transactions downgraded because it batched weekly to dodge a 25 cent batch fee. Settlement dates that did not match authorization dates triggered the downgrades, costing about $1,000 a month to save roughly $2, and the cure was simply daily auto-batching [mqEQN-xgAAk @ 00:04:03]. Eric Jenks of PayTrace puts the timing rule at transactions not settled within 48 hours falling to EIRF, though in the same breath gives a figure of 20 hours, so tighter is safer [AKvayIEwefA @ 00:44:03]. Before any data integration, the operator move is to read the downgrade lines, check batch timing, and quote the gap in dollars the owner can see on their own statement.

The numbers practitioners quote cluster around a one-point spread on Visa commercial cards. PayTrace walks Visa rates from 2.5 to 3 percent down to 1.75 percent with full data, a saving of 75 to 120 basis points [5z1bCzU6Luw @ 00:20:53]. Jenks maps the Visa commercial standard rate of 2.95 percent to Level 2 at 2.05 percent, a 90-point spread worth about $800 in that example, and deliberately skipped modeling a Level 3 move because those Visa cards are not assured to reach it [AKvayIEwefA @ 00:48:15]. Jones cites Visa commercial interchange at 1.9 versus 2.7 percent, an 80 basis point difference before markup, even while headlining the same video with cuts of 1 percent and more [QBl05xxHst0 @ 00:01:27]. Jones's client case is the loudest proof point: an e-commerce merchant whose commercial transactions landed at 2.95, 2.65, 3 and 2.8 moved to 1.45 on large tickets and about 1.9 at Level 2, for savings Jones reports as $35,000 per month [EQEdEkxVIXU @ 00:01:14]. Jenks's example is the conservative template for a proposal: model the Level 2 move first, treat Level 3 as upside, and multiply the spread against commercial volume only, never the merchant's full processing book.

Visa's Commercial Enhanced Data Program rewired the mechanics. TouchSuite reports processors passing through a 0.05 percent participation fee on US commercial and small business transactions sent with Level 2 or Level 3 data, charged whether or not a lower rate applies, and says that since April 2026 sending data may cost more than sending none at all [mFDxx7C-_EA @ 00:00:02]. Verified merchants get Product 3 rates at settlement, while non-verified merchants pay the higher rate up front and see the difference credited back roughly 10 to 15 days later if the data passes [mFDxx7C-_EA @ 00:00:56]. Layton explains what Visa is screening for: its AI flags repeated or generic values in the enhanced data fields, so recycled filler is exactly what gets caught [KlaksrooZhw @ 00:17:35]. PayTrace's answer is a product list tool holding five fields per product, a one-time setup it pegs at about half an hour, after which genuine line-item data rides along with each transaction [5z1bCzU6Luw @ 00:30:53]. The working sequence is consistent across these operators: build a real product catalog, pass clean line items long enough to become verified, then watch settlement and credit-backs to confirm Product 3 rates are actually landing rather than assuming the gateway handled it.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether Level 3 is something a processor simply switches on. Sean Jones of Revolution Payments pitches an interchange audit that will 'automatically update all of your transactions' to Level 3, and says businesses are finding one to one-and-a-half percent added to bottom-line profit margins on their existing sales volume [vVvGM8Rlor8 @ 00:01:23]. Eric Jenks of PayTrace, working the same B2B lane on the CCSalesPro live event, refuses to model it that way. His Visa commercial example moves a 2.95% standard rate only to Level 2 at 2.05%, a 90-point spread worth about $800, because those Visa cards 'don't guarantee to go to level three' [AKvayIEwefA @ 00:48:15]. PayTrace's own CEDP session hardens that into a flat rule: if the merchant is not verified, it does not get Level 3 regardless of what data it tries to send in [5z1bCzU6Luw @ 00:26:40]. TouchSuite adds the cash-flow mechanics behind that rule. Non-Verified merchants pay the higher rate up front at settlement and only see the Product 3 difference credited back roughly 10 to 15 days later, and only if Visa's checks pass the line items [mFDxx7C-_EA @ 00:00:56]. Jones sells the automatic version; Jenks, PayTrace and TouchSuite quote the verified-only version, and the two numbers cannot sit in the same proposal.

Practitioners also disagree on how big the prize actually is. Revolution Payments headlines Level 3 as cutting interchange 'by 1% and more,' yet the same video's worked Visa commercial number is 1.9% against 2.7%, an 80 basis point gap before any markup, and Jones adds that processors earn nothing from interchange, which is why so few of them ever bring it up [QBl05xxHst0 @ 00:01:27]. His own client case swings far wider: before rates of 2.95, 2.65, 3% and 2.8 dropped to 1.45 on large tickets and about 1.9 at Level 2, for a claimed $35,000 per month in savings on an e-commerce merchant [EQEdEkxVIXU @ 00:01:14]. PayTrace frames the Visa win as 2.5 to 3% falling to 1.75%, a saving in the 75 to 120 basis point range [5z1bCzU6Luw @ 00:20:53]. TouchSuite's deliberately made-up example runs much smaller: $100,000 a month in card sales, 40% on business cards, a $1,250 average ticket keyed into a virtual terminal, an assumed 0.5% rate gap, and about $200 a month or $2,400 a year affected by enhanced data [60QTYm0QFZU @ 00:01:31]. Jones sells the ceiling, TouchSuite models the floor, and PayTrace publishes a range an agent can defend line by line in front of a CFO.

The third fault line is who gets paid for the savings and how hard to push the data. Jeremy Layton of VeraSave says the only way his firm makes money is bringing a savings to a merchant: it takes a portion of savings for a set period, charges nothing if nothing is found, and he admits the model has caused contention with processors [KlaksrooZhw @ 00:07:21]. James Sheppard argues from the agent's seat instead. He says he could either cut his residuals and lose margin by lowering pricing, or find a way to cut the interchange costs 'which didn't cost me anything' [AKvayIEwefA @ 00:33:36]. On data integrity the two CCSalesPro voices openly diverge. Sheppard says Visa's CEDP screening could be gamed within a couple of months, and he expected ERP transaction IDs to become mandatory to close that hole [KlaksrooZhw @ 00:20:31]. Layton counters with what he sees in the field: some gateways and acquirers are still inserting randomized fake data into transactions and taking a share of the resulting savings, and he warns of 'big problems' for them if they get caught [KlaksrooZhw @ 00:22:09]. Sheppard's read is that the screening is beatable; Layton's read is that whoever is beating it is carrying the risk on behalf of every merchant in the portfolio.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive mistakes are self-inflicted settlement habits. CCSalesPro's auto shop case is the cleanest example: a merchant doing over $100,000 a month batched weekly to dodge a 25-cent batch fee, the settlement date stopped matching the authorization date, 80% of its transactions downgraded, and the shop burned roughly $1,000 a month to save about $2 until daily auto-batching was switched on [mqEQN-xgAAk @ 00:04:03]. Eric Jenks puts a clock on the same trap, telling agents that transactions not settled within 48 hours fall to EIRF, although in the same answer he also says 20 hours, so the exact window he gives is inconsistent [AKvayIEwefA @ 00:44:03]. Roger McNamara flags a quieter trigger on the CCSalesPro Level 2 and 3 session: a missing sequential invoice number knocks a B2B ticket from roughly 2.05 up to about 2.25 [tG2nIK3Th4Q @ 00:12:28]. TouchSuite's statement checklist stacks up the rest of the usual suspects: zero or missing tax amounts, blank PO numbers, line items that do not sum to the charged total, batches that are not settled promptly, and gateway fields left optional, off by default or unmapped, all under the blunt reminder that 'sending data is not the same as qualifying' [60QTYm0QFZU @ 00:00:55].

Visa's CEDP rollout turned enhanced data from a free upgrade into a trap. Layton reports the program went live October 17, 2025 with Visa tight-lipped on details, and that Visa then paused reviews on November 11 in a rollout he calls 'utter chaos' [KlaksrooZhw @ 00:17:55]. What merchants actually hit was worse than a pause: verified status flipping within one to two weeks, and real line-item data getting flagged as fake [KlaksrooZhw @ 00:19:42]. TouchSuite lays out the cost side. Processors report a 0.05% participation fee on US commercial and small business transactions sent with Level 2 or Level 3 data whether or not a lower rate applies, and since Visa retired Level 2 programs for Business, Corporate and Purchasing cards in mid-April 2026, leaving only fleet fuel, sending Level 2 only can trigger the fee with no rate benefit at all [mFDxx7C-_EA @ 00:00:40]. Its hypothetical distributor, with $100,000 a month in Visa commercial volume, a $1,000 average ticket and zero card-present volume, pays about $2,790 a month on Level 2 only, roughly $600 a year more than sending no data, against about $1,980 a month once verified for Product 3 [mFDxx7C-_EA @ 00:01:34]. The old easy win is now the line item that bleeds.

The economics check that trips up most merchants is whether savings ever reach them. Merchant Doctor warns that some processors simply will not pass Durbin debit savings through, and that qualified, mid-qualified and non-qualified lines on a statement are the tell that a merchant needs to demand true interchange-plus [Hx-TboJVDyo @ 00:02:58]. Sloan Bush of Interchange Plus Solutions puts numbers on the skim: e-commerce debit interchange of 1.6% plus 15 cents, merchants on tiered plans still paying about 2 and a quarter percent plus 30 cents, and tiered processors pocketing the 1.6% savings [LjfmC9EATic @ 00:06:24]. The debit rule itself is a moving target. LawLens reports the 8th Circuit's unanimous October 26, 2026 ruling that knocked out how the Fed built the Regulation II cap, but no new fee was set, the Fed has about 45 days to seek rehearing, and until the mandate issues the 21-cent cap stands and checkout costs do not move [M4iOZn_3wng @ 00:04:36]. On the B2B side the bottleneck is the merchant's own back office: Jenks reports prospects refusing optimization outright because they are locked into a million-dollar ERP system that nobody wants to touch for a payments project [AKvayIEwefA @ 00:55:16].

chapters.question_prompt: How do cash discount and dual pricing programs work, and how do you pitch them to merchants without scaring them off?
chapters.title: Dual Pricing and Cash Discount: Mechanics and the Sales Pitch
chapters.subtitle: How cash discount and dual pricing work on POS systems; free-POS packages; 3% and 4% Edge programs; pros, cons, and worked examples; presenting cash discounting without confusing the merchant; field closing tactics; and cash discount residuals as the key variable
chapters.executive_summary: Dual pricing and cash discounting sellers converge on one promise: post a cash price and a card price, let the customer choose, and push processing cost off the merchant's statement. The gas pump is the universal proof point, used by Joe Wagner, James Shepherd, FTx POS and Titan to normalize the spread, typically three to four percent. On the register, a Valor terminal turns a $100 cash price into a $104 card price; PaymentCloud prices a $17.66 cheeseburger at $18.37 on card. Shepherd warns that residuals live or die on average ticket: $25 to $70 is the sweet spot, a $10 ticket goes negative 20 basis points at 3 percent, and high-ticket corporate reward cards near 2.5 percent interchange squeeze margin. They split on whether shelves must carry both prices and on trial length, from 30 to 60 days.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus — Two Prices, the Gas Pump Frame, and a Zero-Fee Statement
paragraphs: Across the operators, the core mechanism is the same: the merchant posts a cash price and a card price, the customer picks, and the spread covers processing so the merchant stops absorbing fees. Chad The POS Guy frames it bluntly, saying the cash price is always lower and the whole point is that 'your customer pays for the fees, and not you' [pNxf7ZuEt5w @ 00:00:34]. Electronic Money Company sells the same outcome as a merchant statement showing no fees at month end, with card revenue arriving at full value and clients reporting 10 to 30% increases in profit margins [QxwC71KUT-g @ 00:02:36]. Joe Wagner's Easy Pay material pitches offsetting up to 100% of processing fees, naming the specific bleed points merchants hate: percentages, transaction fees, batch fees, statement fees, PCI fees and annual fees [81tAw0Al6N0 @ 00:00:34]. Titan Merchant Services adds the fairness angle, arguing that interchange subsidizes consumer reward programs, so every customer eats year-after-year price hikes driven by someone else's rewards card, while dual pricing hands cash payers a three to four percent break and brings that same three to four percent back to the business [lsC_M7zjTjY @ 00:01:26]. The shared promise is not a lower rate; it is removing the processing line from the merchant's cost structure entirely.

The single most repeated proof point is the fuel pump. Joe Wagner tells merchants that a gas station charging an extra five or ten cents per gallon on a card is the exact program they already accept as consumers, then jokes that nobody drives to another station over a dime [KRZuPsngOLw @ 00:02:18]. James Shepherd of CCSalesPro, after field-selling in rural Pennsylvania, calls the fuel station concept the thread that ties the whole pitch together: it works as the opener, the psychological preamble before objections, the rebuttal itself and the education the merchant later repeats to customers [3bPRCy508Lc @ 00:07:13]. FTx POS points to the same pump sign reading cash price and credit price as the textbook example of dual pricing [YyYXmSsR5as @ 00:01:39]. On customer acceptance, the sellers are uniformly confident. Scott Shaw tells merchants who fear the added four percent will drive shoppers elsewhere that studies show cash discounting was not an issue at the point of sale 99.2 percent of the time and had zero impact on sales, and backs that with a 60-day trial plus a promise to switch back to traditional processing on request [hdPpKRl1Bhk @ 00:02:43]. The consensus: consumer familiarity, not technology, closes the merchant.

Operators also agree on the baseline prerequisites. First, the platform has to support it: Chad The POS Guy warns that Toast and Square cannot pass fees to the customer, so merchants on those systems are forced to eat the roughly 3 percent [pNxf7ZuEt5w @ 00:00:48]. Second, the terminal does the math, not the cashier. Joe Wagner's Easy Pay pitch says the free terminal automatically recognizes payment type, prints the correct cash or credit price on the receipt and tracks everything so there is no reconciliation work [9ImWZ__BWMs @ 00:01:03]. Third, signage and price display: FTx POS insists you must display the credit price and cannot show only the cheaper cash price and then charge more at checkout, because that is just a surcharge by another name [YyYXmSsR5as @ 00:01:56], while O3 Merchant Services' Tanya lists menus, signs, point of sale screens and itemized receipts as places prices must appear [y6h2-zKFtQ0 @ 00:02:04]. Fourth, the commercial wrapper: nearly every seller leads with free equipment and no long-term contract, asking the merchant for a 45 to 60 day test run rather than a lease. Joe Wagner's own line is that merchants stay because they are happy, not because they are locked in.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers — Register Math, Residual Math, and the Scripted Close
paragraphs: The register math is simple and the practitioners show it to the cent. On a Valor PayTech terminal, James Shepherd has the merchant key in only the cash price; the terminal applies the differential, usually four percent, and displays cash price 100, card price 104, with the receipt printing just card price 104 once the card option is chosen [3bPRCy508Lc @ 00:03:30]. Scott Shaw's signage tells customers a four percent fee applies to all store sales with an immediate four percent cash discount, so a ten dollar item rings up at ten dollars cash or ten dollars and forty cents on a card [hdPpKRl1Bhk @ 00:01:19]. PaymentCloud's cafe example lists a bacon cheeseburger at $17.66 cash and $18.37 card, a spread of about 4.02 percent, with both prices on the POS screen and at the bottom of the receipt [xRGCXR9kPug @ 00:01:13]. On the merchant's side of the ledger, Chad The POS Guy runs $30,000 a month at about 3 percent: $900 out of pocket and $29,100 taken home under traditional processing, versus the full $30,000 under dual pricing [pNxf7ZuEt5w @ 00:01:07]. Shepherd stresses the back end is identical to a non-cash adjustment program; only display, receipt and signage change.

For the ISO side, James Shepherd calls average ticket the most important variable in cash discounting residuals, because the program is really flat rate pricing: the rep earns on the service fee collected from card payers, not on the discount [AnhJYbY3ptw @ 00:00:20]. The sweet spot is a $25 to $70 average ticket. Signature debit carries regulated interchange of 22 cents plus 5 basis points, roughly 30 to 32 cents all-in with processor fees, which is only about 1 percent on a $30 sale, so a 3 percent service fee leaves around 180 basis points of markup [AnhJYbY3ptw @ 00:02:07]. That debit math matters in practice: FTx POS reports that over 80 percent of its parent company's card transactions flag as debit [YyYXmSsR5as @ 00:00:58]. The edges bite. At a $10 ticket the 32 cents becomes 3.2 percent, so a 3 percent fee yields residuals of negative 20 basis points; at $5 it is 6.4 percent, underwater even at 3.99 percent, which is why Shepherd suggests a per-item fee like 59 cents on tiny tickets. At $150 tickets, jewelry and B2B merchants may run corporate reward cards near 2.5 percent interchange, so the percentage has to climb [AnhJYbY3ptw @ 00:04:26].

The sales sequence is equally scripted. Joe Wagner's four-step soft-blow method runs: make them feel the savings, normalize it through the gas pump, explain that the program works exactly that way, then pull out the application with 'here let me show you,' a line Wagner says will make some reps millions [KRZuPsngOLw @ 00:04:02]. Inside the longer five-step conversation of intro, short story, presentation, close and rehash, Wagner refuses to ask for the bill, instead offering an either-or ballpark like 'are you paying like 700 a month here, are you more like in the 400 range,' then annualizing a $500 answer into $6,000 a year and asking what the merchant would do with it [tgxPcd70hpA @ 00:09:26]. The application's first page shows annual, batch and transaction fees crossed out with black X's, which doubles as the bridge into the presentation and then into the close [tgxPcd70hpA @ 00:06:24]. James Shepherd's field opener skips the curiosity hook entirely: ask whether the merchant has seen a fuel station with cash and card prices, then explain that their current price becomes the cash price and the company 'just collects that tiny little difference' to offset processing [3bPRCy508Lc @ 00:06:11]. Shepherd reports a really good response to that opener.

callout.title: Closing Lines and Pricing Tweaks the Pros Actually Use
callout.body: Field-tested moves from reps who have closed dual pricing and cash discount deals door to door and priced them for residuals.
items: Always annualize the savings: a merchant saving $500 a month hears 'six thousand dollars a year,' then gets asked whether it goes back into the business or toward a vacation [Joe Wagner | Merchant Services & Passive Income — KRZuPsngOLw @ 00:01:14].

Never ask for the statement; say 'I don't even need your bill' because the fees are going away, and let the merchant ballpark with an either-or question [Joe Wagner | Merchant Services & Passive Income — tgxPcd70hpA @ 00:09:10].
On very low tickets, swap the 3.99 percent service fee for a per-item fee such as 59 cents, and on high-ticket corporate card merchants push the percentage up [CCSalesPro — AnhJYbY3ptw @ 00:03:45].

Once you are filling out the application, stop explaining; Wagner says these deals are so fragile one small extra detail triggers ten more rebuttals [Joe Wagner | Merchant Services & Passive Income — tgxPcd70hpA @ 00:24:41].

sop_steps.title: Intro That Kills Rebuttals Up Front
sop_steps.action: Open likable and short, pre-empting the 'I'm busy' and 'I get calls all day' brush-offs before the merchant can use them.
sop_steps.detail: Wagner's opener is 'I know you're real busy and I probably get like two calls on this a day, let me just share what I've got and I'll be out of your way,' because people buy when they like and trust you [Joe Wagner | Merchant Services & Passive Income — tgxPcd70hpA @ 00:01:44].

sop_steps.title: Feel the Savings, Then Normalize at the Pump
sop_steps.action: Get a ballpark monthly fee figure, annualize it, then walk the merchant back to the last time they paid a higher card price for gas.
sop_steps.detail: Ask about the gas station charging five or ten cents more per gallon on a card and joke that nobody drives elsewhere over a dime, so the merchant remembers being the consumer and not flinching [Joe Wagner | Merchant Services & Passive Income — KRZuPsngOLw @ 00:02:18].

sop_steps.title: Pull the App Out as a Trust Tool
sop_steps.action: Show the first page with annual, batch and transaction fees crossed out, pull the free terminal form, and write the core model on the paper.
sop_steps.detail: Wagner writes 'month to month, no contract' on the application and offers an initial next to it, so the words match a document and the rep is already bridging into the close [Joe Wagner | Merchant Services & Passive Income — tgxPcd70hpA @ 00:18:07].

sop_steps.title: Bridge Close, Handshake and Rehash
sop_steps.action: Deliver a bridge close line, stick a hand out for the handshake, then confirm signage, install timing and the referral ask.
sop_steps.detail: Line: 'The hardest part is what we're doing right here, it only takes another couple of minutes'; then signage ships, the pre-programmed terminal arrives in five to seven days, and the rep warns they will come back for referrals [Joe Wagner | Merchant Services & Passive Income — tgxPcd70hpA @ 00:25:39].

sections.heading: 3. Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first fault line is what the product actually is. PaymentCloud draws a hard line: a cash discount knocks a discount off the regular price when the customer pays cash, while dual pricing runs two separate prices with the cash price sitting as the original sticker price [xRGCXR9kPug @ 00:01:54]. James Shepherd of CCSalesPro flattens that distinction on the money side, telling reps that this version of dual pricing has the exact same economic model as a non-cash adjustment or service fee program, so residuals and margin do not move at all; only the display, signage and receipt print change. Shepherd's reason for switching is card-brand pressure: Visa has come out strongly against adding a fee line item to the receipt, so the customer now picks a cash or card price before the card ever touches the terminal [3bPRCy508Lc @ 00:02:08]. Scott Shaw still pitches the older structure openly, with signage announcing a four percent fee on all store sales and software that adds a four percent service fee at checkout, turning a $10 item into $10.40 on a card [hdPpKRl1Bhk @ 00:01:00]. Joe Wagner sidesteps the labels entirely and sells the whole thing as flat-rate processing with the junk fees crossed out [tgxPcd70hpA @ 00:03:12].

The second split is how much shelf work the merchant has to do. Tanya at O3 Merchant Services tells owners they must display prices everywhere, on menus, signs, point of sale screens and itemized receipts, before running the program [y6h2-zKFtQ0 @ 00:02:04]. Shepherd pushes back on blanket shelf rules: what the merchant puts on the shelf or menu is the merchant's decision, the terminal keys in only the cash price and calculates a card price usually four percent higher, and only certain states such as New York truly require both prices on the shelf or menu [3bPRCy508Lc @ 00:04:09]. FTx POS lands in the middle with one bright line: you must display the credit price, and showing only the cheaper cash price then charging more at checkout is just another way of doing a surcharge [YyYXmSsR5as @ 00:01:56]. On surcharging itself, PaymentCloud says it carries many regulations and state rules while dual pricing does not [xRGCXR9kPug @ 00:02:28], and FTx goes further, saying dual pricing has no caps, works in all 50 states, and lets a merchant discount as deep as they want, whereas surcharging is capped at 3% or actual cost and blocked on every debit card, which FTx says covers over 80% of card transactions in its parent company stores.

The economics of the merchant-facing offer also diverge. Joe Wagner's Easy Pay model charges one flat monthly fee for the life of the account: $25 under $5,000 in volume, $50 between $5,000 and $10,000, and a flat $100 above $10,000, no matter whether the merchant runs $50,000 or $100,000 [81tAw0Al6N0 @ 00:01:38]. iSmart Payments' Edge pitch goes lower, claiming most businesses processing over $10,000 a month pay zero, with software that knows in real time what each non-cash transaction will cost and adjusts the purchase price to offset it [x7WUlpG34a8 @ 00:01:46]. Customer reaction is the other live argument. Scott Shaw's pitch claims studies show cash discounting was not an issue 99.2 percent of the time and had zero impact on sales [hdPpKRl1Bhk @ 00:02:43], while PaymentCloud lists customer confusion and extra staff explaining time as real costs and warns that too wide a cash-card gap can discourage sales if customers see the card price as unfair [xRGCXR9kPug @ 00:03:36]. Shaw backs the claim with a 60-day trial and a promise to switch merchants back to traditional processing while still paying less than they do now. PaymentCloud's answer is the opposite lever: strike a balance between the cash incentive and a reasonable card price, and treat customer communication as the key to making the program work.
